title: Greetings & Introductions
objectives: Greet people formally and informally
Introduce yourself by name
Use Austrian-specific greetings like Servus and Grüß Gott

grammar.explanation: German has formal (Sie) and informal (du) 'you'. In Tirol, locals are very friendly and often jump to 'du' fast — but use 'Sie' first with strangers, older people, and in shops.

culturalNote: In Tirol locals shift to 'du' fast, but use 'Sie' first in shops and with strangers. Grüß Gott and Servus are more Austrian than German.

title: Numbers 1–20
objectives: Count from 1 to 20 in German
Understand the reversed structure of compound numbers (21–99)

grammar.explanation: Numbers 21–99 are 'backwards' in German: 21 = einundzwanzig = 'one and twenty'. Same in Tyrolean dialect, just sounds different.

title: Ordering Food & Drink
objectives: Order food and drinks at a café or restaurant
Ask for the bill in the Austrian way
Know the genders of common food nouns

grammar.explanation: German nouns have three genders: der (masc), die (fem), das (neut). You MUST learn the article with the noun. There is no shortcut.

examples.de: Ich möchte ein Bier und die Rechnung, bitte.
examples.en: I would like a beer and the bill, please.

culturalNote: Zahlen, bitte is the Austrian way to ask for the bill — you'll hear it everywhere. Mahlzeit is used as a greeting around lunchtime, not just at the table.

title: Days, Time, Weather
objectives: Name the days of the week
Tell the time using 'halb' correctly
Describe basic weather conditions

grammar.explanation: To say time: 'Es ist drei Uhr' = It is three o'clock. 'Halb drei' = 2:30 (literally 'half three' — meaning halfway TO three). This trips up English speakers.

examples.de: Heute ist Montag und es schneit.
examples.en: Today is Monday and it is snowing.

culturalNote: Austrians say Samstag, not Sonnabend (common in northern Germany). Snow vocab is essential — Tirol gets a lot of it.

title: Getting Around Tirol
objectives: Ask where things are using 'Wo ist…?'
Name key transport options in Tirol
Give and understand basic directions

grammar.explanation: Question words: Wer (who), Was (what), Wo (where), Wann (when), Warum (why), Wie (how). All start with W. Easy to remember.

examples.en: Where is the cable car, please?

culturalNote: The Bergbahn (mountain cable car) is a key part of getting around Tirol year-round — skiing in winter, hiking in summer. Die Hütte is not just a hut, it's a mountain restaurant on the slopes.

title: Shopping & Prices
objectives: Ask how much something costs
Express that something is too expensive
Understand the accusative case for masculine nouns

grammar.explanation: The accusative case: when something is the object of a verb, masculine 'der' changes to 'den'. Die and das stay the same. Example: 'Ich kaufe den Apfel' (masc.) but 'Ich kaufe die Birne' (fem.) and 'Ich kaufe das Brot' (neut.).

examples.en: I buy the pear. (fem. stays die)

examples.de: Wie viel kostet das? — Zu teuer. Haben Sie etwas Günstigeres?
examples.en: How much does that cost? — Too expensive. Do you have something cheaper?

culturalNote: Innsbruck's Markthalle is a great place to practice shopping German. Markets run on cash — have coins ready.

title: At the Hotel
objectives: Check in and check out at a hotel
Request room types and ask what's available
Use modal verbs (können, müssen) correctly

grammar.point: Modal verbs + infinitive at the end
grammar.explanation: Modal verbs: können (can), müssen (must), wollen (want), dürfen (may). They always pair with an infinitive at the end of the sentence. 'Ich kann Deutsch sprechen.' — I can speak German.

examples.de: Ich möchte ein Doppelzimmer für zwei Nächte, bitte.
examples.en: I would like a double room for two nights, please.

culturalNote: Austrian hotels almost always include breakfast (Frühstück). If it's not mentioned, ask: 'Ist das Frühstück inklusive?'
